cards.front: Where do a plant's new cells come from, and what happens to the daughter cells?
cards.back: From meristems, groups of cells that keep dividing. The daughters then grow and take on their final types.
cards.quote: A plant's new cells come from its meristems, groups of cells that keep dividing; their daughters then grow and take on their final types.

cards.front: Along a root: length added per hour = new cells per file (a lengthwise row of cells) per hour × {{c1::final cell length}}.
cards.back: Growth depends on how many cells a meristem makes and how big each one grows.
cards.quote: Along a root: length added per hour = new cells per file (a lengthwise row of cells) per hour × final cell length.

cards.front: When is the root rule (length per hour = new cells per file per hour × final cell length) exact, and why is it not a forecast?
cards.back: Only at steady state with every cell file alike. It is geometry, not a forecast: real growth changes with age, season and site.
cards.quote: Scope: the root rule is exact only at steady state with every file alike.

cards.front: In a tree, what adds height and what adds the trunk's wood and most of its width?
cards.back: Height comes from young shoots near the tips (apical meristems). The wood and most of the added width come from the vascular cambium.
cards.why: The vascular cambium runs the same division-times-size rule sideways.
cards.quote: In a tree, height comes from young shoots near the tips; the trunk's wood and most of its added width come from the vascular cambium

cards.front: Name the three organs of a flowering plant and the main job of each.
cards.back: Root: anchors and absorbs water and minerals. Stem: holds up leaves, buds and flowers and connects them to the roots. Leaf: main site of photosynthesis in most plants.
cards.quote: the root anchors it and absorbs water and minerals, the stem holds up leaves, buds and flowers and connects them to the roots
cards.section: A map of the plant body

cards.front: Name the three tissue systems of a plant and what each does.
cards.back: Dermal: covers the plant (epidermis in a young plant). Vascular: carries water and minerals in xylem, sugars and amino acids in phloem. Ground: everything else; stores, supports and, in green parts, photosynthesizes.
cards.quote: Each organ is built from the same three tissue systems, sets of tissues that run through the whole plant.
cards.section: A map of the plant body

cards.front: In plant anatomy, distinguish a cell type, a tissue and a tissue system.
cards.back: A cell type is one kind of cell; a tissue is a group of cells working together; a tissue system is a plant-wide set of tissues.
cards.quote: a cell type is one kind of cell, a tissue a group of cells working together, a tissue system a plant-wide set of tissues.
cards.section: A map of the plant body

cards.front: Where are apical meristems, and what kind of growth do they produce?
cards.back: At the tips of growing roots and shoots. They produce primary growth, mainly growth in length.
cards.quote: Apical meristems lie at the tips of growing roots and shoots and produce primary growth, mainly growth in length
cards.section: Growing from the tips: division, then elongation

cards.front: A root cortex cell file delivers 1 new cell per hour, and cells mature at 300 micrometers. Assuming steady state and all files alike, how fast does the root grow per day?
cards.back: 1 cell/h × 300 µm × 24 h = 7,200 µm = 7.2 mm per day.
cards.quote: Each row is cells per hour x final length x 24 hours: 1 x 300 micrometers x 24 = 7.2 mm per day.
cards.section: Growing from the tips: division, then elongation

cards.front: In the same root (1 new cell per file per hour, cells leave the meristem at 15 micrometers and normally mature at 300 micrometers), elongation is blocked but division is unchanged. Predict the growth rate and what it says about elongation.
cards.back: Growth falls to 1 × 15 µm × 24 h = 0.36 mm per day, one twentieth of the normal 7.2 mm per day. Elongation supplies most of the root's length.
cards.quote: Blocked elongation leaves growth at one twentieth of normal, so elongation supplies most of the length.
cards.section: Growing from the tips: division, then elongation

cards.front: Root A divides at half the normal rate (0.5 cells per file per hour) with cells reaching 300 micrometers. Root B divides normally (1 per hour) and grows at the same rate as A. What changed in B, and can growth rate alone tell the two apart?
cards.back: B's cells reach only 150 µm: 1 × 150 = 0.5 × 300 = 150 µm per hour (3.6 mm per day). No: you also need the rate of new cells or the final length.
cards.quote: So no: growth rate alone cannot tell you whether division or elongation changed; you also need the rate of new cells or the final length.
cards.section: Growing from the tips: division, then elongation

cards.front: Each cell file of a seedling root delivers 2 new cells per hour, and cells reach a final length of 250 micrometers. Assuming steady state and all files alike, what is the growth rate in mm per day?
cards.back: 2 cells/h × 250 µm = 500 µm per hour; × 24 h = 12,000 µm = 12 mm per day.
cards.quote: Each row is cells per hour x final length x 24 hours
cards.section: Growing from the tips: division, then elongation

cards.front: A drug stops all cell division in a root's apical meristem but does not affect elongation of cells already made. Predict root growth over the next days.
cards.back: Growth continues briefly as cells already made finish elongating and mature, then stops, because no new cells arrive.
cards.why: Growth depends on both how many cells the meristem makes and how big each grows; with zero new cells, the product goes to zero.
cards.quote: Growth depends on how many cells a meristem makes and how big each one grows.

cards.front: A shoot tip starts one or more leaves at each node, with a bud in the angle of each leaf; the stretches of stem between nodes are {{c1::internodes}}.
cards.quote: the stretches of stem between its nodes are internodes
cards.section: Growing from the tips: division, then elongation

cards.front: How does the way many plants build their bodies differ from most animals?
cards.back: Plant meristems keep dividing, so many plants add new organs for years. Most animals lay down their body plan early, though many keep growing in size.
cards.why: Not every meristem lasts: in maize the shoot apex finally becomes the tassel.
cards.quote: Most animals, by contrast, lay down their body plan early (see animal development), though many keep growing in size.
cards.section: Growing from the tips: division, then elongation

cards.front: In the Datura shoot-tip experiments, how were cells marked so that every descendant carried the mark?
cards.back: Colchicine doubled the chromosome number of some cells; doubled cells and their offspring are larger, so they show up in a section.
cards.why: Seeds were soaked in colchicine; sometimes only one layer was doubled, giving a periclinal chimera.
cards.quote: Colchicine, a drug that stops chromosomes separating, doubles a cell's chromosome number, and doubled cells and their offspring are larger
cards.section: Growing from the tips: division, then elongation

cards.front: A Datura shoot tip has only its outermost layer doubled (larger cells). If cells of the tip mixed as they divided, where would large cells appear? What was actually seen, and what does it show?
cards.back: Mixing would scatter large cells through many tissues. Instead, large cells appeared in the epidermis and not beneath it: the apex has three layers that stay separate.
cards.quote: Instead, a doubled outermost layer gave large cells in the epidermis and not in the tissues beneath.
cards.section: Growing from the tips: division, then elongation

cards.front: In the Datura shoot apex, what does each of the layers L1, L2 and L3 make?
cards.back: L1: the epidermis. L2: most of the tissue just under it in leaves and flowers, including the cells that make pollen and eggs. L3: the stem's inner core and its vascular tissue.
cards.quote: L1 makes the epidermis; L2 makes most of the tissue just under it in leaves and flowers
cards.section: Growing from the tips: division, then elongation

cards.front: A Datura periclinal chimera has only its L2 layer doubled. Predict whether its leaf epidermis and its pollen come from doubled cells.
cards.back: The epidermis is not doubled, but the pollen is: L2 makes the cells that go on to make pollen and eggs, while L1 makes the epidermis.
cards.why: Rests on the clonally separate layers and their fates.
cards.quote: L2 makes most of the tissue just under it in leaves and flowers, including the cells that go on to make pollen and eggs
cards.section: Growing from the tips: division, then elongation

cards.front: Does every plant shoot apex have three clonally separate layers like Datura?
cards.back: No. Maize and some other grasses have two, and in many species a neighbouring cell occasionally invades a layer.
cards.quote: That does not mean three layers in every plant: maize and some other grasses have two
cards.section: Growing from the tips: division, then elongation

cards.front: Contrast parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma cells by living state, walls and role.
cards.back: Parenchyma: living, thin-walled general workers. Collenchyma: living, unevenly thickened walls, flexible support for young stems and leaves. Sclerenchyma: thick secondary walls hardened with lignin; fibers and sclereids.
cards.quote: Collenchyma cells are living, with unevenly thickened walls, and give flexible support to young stems and leaves
cards.section: What the meristems' cells become

cards.front: A student finds a short cell in pear flesh with a thick secondary wall hardened with lignin. Which of the three general cell classes is it, and which form?
cards.back: Sclerenchyma, as a sclereid (the grit in a pear). Long sclerenchyma cells would be fibers.
cards.quote: They come as long fibers and as shorter sclereids (the grit in a pear).
cards.section: What the meristems' cells become

cards.front: Why are xylem and phloem called tissues rather than cell types?
cards.back: Each is a complex tissue made of several cell types: xylem includes tracheids and vessel elements; phloem includes sieve-tube elements and companion cells.
cards.quote: Xylem and phloem are not cell types but complex tissues, each made of several.
cards.section: What the meristems' cells become

cards.front: How does water pass along vessel elements compared with tracheids?
cards.back: Vessel elements join end to end through open perforations to form pipes; water passes between tracheids through thin pits in their walls. Both are dead at maturity.
cards.quote: Vessel elements join end to end through open perforations to form pipes; water passes between tracheids through thin pits in their walls.
cards.section: What the meristems' cells become

cards.front: In a flowering plant, a conducting cell is alive at maturity, has no nucleus and sits beside a supporting cell. Name the cell, its partner, and the tissue it belongs to.
cards.back: A sieve-tube element, supported by a companion cell, in the phloem. It carries sugars. Xylem conducting cells, by contrast, are dead at maturity.
cards.quote: which stay alive at maturity although they lose their nucleus, each supported by a neighbouring companion cell.
cards.section: What the meristems' cells become

cards.front: In a typical eudicot leaf, a waxy {{c1::cuticle}} over the epidermis reduces water loss.
cards.quote: A waxy cuticle over the epidermis reduces water loss.
cards.section: A leaf: what the shoot tip builds at each node

cards.front: Contrast palisade and spongy mesophyll in a typical eudicot leaf.
cards.back: Palisade: tightly packed column-shaped cells full of chloroplasts, under the upper epidermis. Spongy: loosely arranged cells, also with chloroplasts, separated by air spaces that connect to the stomata.
cards.quote: Below it, spongy mesophyll has loosely arranged cells, also with chloroplasts, separated by air spaces that connect to the stomata.
cards.section: A leaf: what the shoot tip builds at each node

cards.front: Why does every gain of carbon cost a leaf water?
cards.back: An open stoma, the pore between two guard cells, lets carbon dioxide in and water vapour out at the same time.
cards.quote: An open stoma lets carbon dioxide in and water vapour out, so every gain of carbon costs water.
cards.section: A leaf: what the shoot tip builds at each node

cards.front: The guard cells of a eudicot leaf close its stomata. Predict what happens to carbon dioxide uptake and to water loss through the pores, and why.
cards.back: Both fall. The same open pore admits carbon dioxide and releases water vapour, so closing it saves water but also stops carbon gain.
cards.quote: Stomata (singular stoma) are pores, each between a pair of guard cells that open and close it.
cards.section: A leaf: what the shoot tip builds at each node

cards.front: What is Kranz anatomy in a maize leaf, and what does it do?
cards.back: Each vein is wrapped in large bundle-sheath cells ringed by mesophyll. It splits carbon fixation (C4) into two steps in two cell types: mesophyll makes a four-carbon acid; bundle-sheath cells release carbon dioxide from it for Rubisco.
cards.why: Kranz anatomy is not required for C4: Bienertia sinuspersici separates the two steps within single cells.
cards.quote: each vein is wrapped in large bundle-sheath cells ringed by mesophyll, a wreath called Kranz anatomy
cards.section: A leaf: what the shoot tip builds at each node

cards.front: Name the two lateral meristems and what each adds in a woody stem.
cards.back: Vascular cambium: secondary xylem (wood) inward and secondary phloem outward. Cork cambium: periderm, the outer part of the bark.
cards.quote: the vascular cambium, which runs the same rule sideways (the cork cambium adds periderm, the outer part of the bark)

cards.front: Define bark in a woody stem. Which tissues does it include?
cards.back: Everything outside the vascular cambium: the secondary phloem and the periderm, plus, in old trunks, older periderms and the dead tissue outside them.
cards.quote: in old trunks bark also includes older periderms and the dead tissue outside them
cards.section: Growing wider: how much wood a ring adds

cards.front: Beetle larvae chew a complete ring through a young tree's secondary phloem but leave the wood intact. Predict what happens to the leaves and to the roots in the following weeks, and why.
cards.back: Leaves stay supplied with water for a time, because xylem (the wood) is intact. Roots are cut off from sugars from the leaves, because phloem carries sugars from the leaves and the ring cut it.
cards.why: Rests on xylem carrying water and minerals and phloem carrying sugars, and on secondary phloem lying outside the cambium.
cards.quote: The vascular system carries water and minerals in xylem and sugars and amino acids in phloem.
cards.section: A map of the plant body

cards.front: A cambium adds a 2 mm ring in a year to a sapling of radius 20 mm and to a trunk of radius 200 mm. How many times more wood (cross-sectional area) does the trunk gain?
cards.back: Trunk: π(202² − 200²) = π × 804 ≈ 2,530 mm². Sapling: π(22² − 20²) = π × 84 ≈ 264 mm². Ratio ≈ 9.6, a little under 10.
cards.why: The added area scales roughly with radius, not radius squared.
cards.quote: So, for the same height of trunk, the area added scales roughly with radius, not radius squared.
cards.section: Growing wider: how much wood a ring adds

cards.front: A trunk of radius 100 mm adds a ring 3 mm wide. Use the mid-ring circumference shortcut to find the cross-sectional area of new wood.
cards.back: 2π × (100 + 1.5) × 3 = 609π ≈ 1,913 mm². This equals the exact π(103² − 100²) = 609π.
cards.quote: The exact area, pi x ((r + w) squared - r squared), equals 2 x pi x (r + w/2) x w for any trunk.
cards.section: Why the circumference at the middle of the ring

cards.front: Why does estimating a ring's area as inner circumference × ring width (2πrw) come out low, and when is the error worst?
cards.back: It ignores that the ring's middle lies at r + w/2, so it undercounts. The error grows as the stem gets thinner: 0.5 percent on a 200 mm trunk, 16.7 percent on a 5 mm twig.
cards.quote: The shortcut 2 x pi x r x w (inner circumference) comes out low: 0.5 percent on the 200 mm trunk
cards.section: Why the circumference at the middle of the ring

cards.front: A tree adds a ring of wood 3 mm wide. If new xylem cells average 50 micrometers wide radially, about how many new cells did each radial file add?
cards.back: 3,000 µm ÷ 50 µm = 60 cells per radial file.
cards.why: Ring width = cells added per file × cell width, the root rule run sideways.
cards.quote: with illustrative xylem cells averaging 40 micrometers wide radially, a 2 mm ring is about 50 new cells per radial file.
cards.section: Growing wider: how much wood a ring adds

cards.front: In a normal year a tree's cambium adds about 50 cells per radial file, each about 40 micrometers wide, giving a 2 mm ring. In a drought year it adds half as many cells of the same width. Predict the ring width, and does the same ring add more wood area on a trunk 10 times wider?
cards.back: 25 × 40 µm = 1 mm ring. Area scales roughly with radius, so the same ring adds a little under 10 times more area on a 10-times-wider trunk.
cards.why: Rests on ring width = cells per file × cell width, and on ring area scaling roughly with radius.
cards.quote: The ring width is itself the one idea's product
cards.section: Growing wider: how much wood a ring adds

cards.front: Maize stems lengthen but never add wood. Which meristems does maize use to lengthen, and which does it lack?
cards.back: Besides its tips, it lengthens from intercalary meristems at the bases of leaves and internodes. It lacks a conventional vascular cambium, so it makes no wood.
cards.quote: intercalary meristems, inserted between mature tissues
cards.section: Growing wider: how much wood a ring adds

cards.front: How does Arabidopsis thaliana grow, and does it ever form a cambium?
cards.back: Mostly by primary growth, but its hypocotyl (the stem below the seed leaves) and its root each form a cambium.
cards.quote: Arabidopsis thaliana, a small herbaceous eudicot, grows mostly by primary growth, though its hypocotyl (the stem below the seed leaves) and its root each form a cambium.
cards.section: Four bodies, one toolkit: herb, tree, grass, cactus

cards.front: Where does a prickly pear cactus (Opuntia) photosynthesize, what are its spines, and when does it open its stomata?
cards.back: In its flattened green stems. Its spines are modified leaves. It uses CAM, opening its stomata mainly at night.
cards.quote: A prickly pear cactus (Opuntia) photosynthesizes in its flattened green stems.
cards.section: Four bodies, one toolkit: herb, tree, grass, cactus

cards.front: Is an oak more advanced than Arabidopsis, maize or a cactus? Why or why not?
cards.back: No. Each lineage has had the same time to evolve; they use one toolkit of meristems and tissues in different ways.
cards.quote: None is more advanced than the others; each lineage has had the same time to evolve.
cards.section: Four bodies, one toolkit: herb, tree, grass, cactus

cards.front: In the Arabidopsis hypocotyl cambium, a permanent fluorescent mark is switched on in a few scattered cells; some marked clones span xylem, cambium and phloem. Why use a permanent mark rather than a pulse label like EdU, and what alternative must be ruled out?
cards.back: A permanent mark is inherited by every descendant, so a clone reaching both xylem and phloem means one lineage made both; EdU dilutes with division. Alternative: two neighbouring cells marked at once.
cards.why: Controls: sparse induction, count adjacent marks in short-term samples, reporter off without inducer.
cards.quote: A permanent lineage mark is inherited by every descendant of the marked cell, so a clone that reaches both xylem and phloem means one cell's lineage made both.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In an Arabidopsis hypocotyl lineage-tracing study followed for 10 days, 35 of 99 marked cambium clones spanned xylem, cambium and phloem. Can you conclude that about 35 percent of cambium cells are stem cells?
cards.back: No. 35 percent is the fraction of this sample of clones; a clone's type depends on which cell was marked and how long it was followed. It also says nothing about oak cambium.
cards.quote: That is the fraction of this sample of clones, not the fraction of cambium cells that are stem cells
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Why does a temperate oak usually show one ring per year, and why is ring-counting not certain?
cards.back: The cambium works in spring and summer and rests in winter; spring wood has large vessels, late-summer wood smaller ones. Some years leave a false extra ring or none.
cards.quote: Some years leave a false extra ring or none, so one ring per year is usual, not certain.
cards.section: Reading a ring
